evals.prompt: I'm starting a new project to simulate a TT&C ground station that needs to track multiple LEO satellites, receive their telemetry, and send commands back up. I know I'll need orbital mechanics, RF link modeling, and protocol handling, but I'm not sure how to organize all this. The ground station should handle automatic antenna pointing, deal with Doppler shift, and decode CCSDS packets. How should I structure this system? What are the main components I need, and in what order should I build them?
evals.expected_output: A comprehensive system decomposition that: (1) Identifies major subsystems (orbital propagation, visibility calculation, antenna control, RF link, telemetry reception, command transmission, CCSDS protocol handling); (2) Defines clear interfaces and data flow between subsystems; (3) Provides an implementation roadmap starting with minimal end-to-end functionality (basic orbit propagation + visibility) before adding complexity (RF effects, Doppler, full CCSDS); (4) Explains dependencies and rationale for build order
expectations: Identifies at least 5-7 major subsystems with distinct responsibilities
Defines inputs and outputs for each subsystem
Provides an implementation roadmap with prioritized build order
Explains why foundational components (orbit propagator, visibility calculator) come first
Addresses all mentioned requirements: multiple satellites, auto-pointing, Doppler, CCSDS
Recommends starting with a minimal working system before full features

evals.prompt: I need to build a satellite simulation that includes attitude control (reaction wheels and magnetorquers), power management (solar panels and batteries tracking sun angle and eclipse periods), and thermal management (heaters controlled based on component temperatures). These all interact—attitude affects which solar panels see the sun, which affects power, which affects whether I can run heaters. I'm overwhelmed by the coupling. How do I break this down into something I can actually implement?
evals.expected_output: A decomposition strategy that: (1) Identifies the core dependencies (attitude → solar panel orientation → power generation → available power → thermal control decisions); (2) Proposes separation of concerns (attitude dynamics separate from power calculations separate from thermal model, but with clear data flow); (3) Suggests a central state management approach or event-driven architecture to handle cross-cutting interactions; (4) Provides an implementation order that builds one subsystem at a time while stubbing dependencies (e.g., fixed attitude initially, then add attitude dynamics); (5) Addresses the coupling explicitly with architectural patterns
expectations: Acknowledges the coupling between subsystems explicitly
Proposes architectural pattern to manage cross-cutting concerns (e.g., central state, publish-subscribe, event-driven)
Identifies subsystems: Attitude Dynamics, Power System, Thermal System, Orbital/Environmental (sun position, eclipse)
Defines clear data flow showing how attitude affects power which affects thermal
Suggests implementation strategy with stubbed dependencies to enable independent development
Recommends starting with simplified assumptions (e.g., constant sun angle) before adding full complexity

evals.prompt: What components do I need for a basic satellite uplink command system? I want to be able to send commands from a ground station to a satellite, have the satellite validate them, execute them, and send back confirmation. Not looking for a super detailed architecture, just want to understand the main pieces before I start coding.
evals.expected_output: A concise decomposition suitable for a basic system: (1) Identifies 4-6 main components (Command Interface/Input, Command Validator, Command Encoder, Uplink Transmission, Satellite Receiver/Decoder, Command Executor, Confirmation Telemetry); (2) Explains the flow: create command → validate → encode → transmit → receive → decode → execute → confirm; (3) Highlights the critical component (validation) and why it matters; (4) Suggests simple starting point (direct command delivery without RF simulation initially)
expectations: Identifies command lifecycle: creation → validation → encoding → transmission → reception → execution → confirmation
Lists 4-6 main components with clear responsibilities
Emphasizes validation as a critical component for safety
Suggests starting simple (direct delivery) before adding RF link simulation
Mentions encoding (even if simplified initially) and confirmation telemetry
Keeps response concise and appropriate for 'basic' request—not over-engineered
